rationale: B wins because it knows where the floorboards are weak and labels them before anyone falls through. Its line, "Without both halves, this angle is performance and should be dropped," is exactly the discipline this exercise needs. A has good bones, but it smuggles in a whole competitive landscape with "Expedia, Kayak, and Hopper have bolted AI planners" and "everyone else already building the same feature" when the update did not hand it those facts.
gaps_in_A: "Expedia, Kayak, and Hopper have bolted AI planners onto their products" is an invented competitive fact from the supplied update. If that comparison carries Angle 1, it must be sourced, not wished into existence.
"most AI trip planners start from a user's query" is the hinge of the best angle, and it is not in the facts. That turns a promising product-design lens into an unsupported claim.

"The company once known as Scott's Cheap Flights just built an AI travel app" is padded identity-arc material. The update gives the old name, not a rebrand narrative, product-evolution arc, or founder/profile hook.
"A tech reporter or columnist" in the contrarian angle is too loose. The stronger shape is travel-tech/OTA/AI-booking coverage, not generic AI skepticism.
gaps_in_B: "Mistake fares vanish fast" is plausible, but it is not in the supplied facts. The set correctly asks for a named member example, but the headline still states the urgency before proving it.
"category-creation" is inflated. A fare-alert company adding planning is a product expansion story unless there is outside evidence that alert services are becoming a real category of planning tools.

"$550 per flight: the savings number Going's paid tier rests on" leans hard on a company-stated average. B handles the methodology caveat well, but the headline should not imply the whole paid tier rests on that number until Going says or proves it.
